work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Letter attributed to Julian
english: They also say that the marriages now taking place were not instituted by God. This can be read in Augustine’s book, which I have just answered in four short books.
translator_notes: Quoted from the letter attributed to Julian, also preserved in Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 1.5.9. Augustine uses it to identify the likely source of the excerpts sent to him.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Augustine quoted in the intermediary document
english: “They shout against us with the greatest hostility that we condemn marriage and God’s work, by which God creates human beings from males and females, because we say that those born from such union inherit original sin. Whatever parents they are born from, we do not deny that they are still under the devil unless they are born again in Christ.”
translator_notes: This is Augustine’s text as quoted in the intermediary document. Augustine says the document omitted his citation of Romans 5:12 at this point. It is not Julian’s own profession of belief.
“Born again in Christ” echoes the teaching about new birth in John 3:3–5.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Augustine quoted in the intermediary document
english: “They do not notice that the good of marriage cannot be accused because of the original evil derived from it, just as the evil of adultery and sexual immorality cannot be excused because of the natural good born from it. For just as sin, whether derived from the one or the other, is the devil’s work, so a human being, whether born from the one or the other, is God’s work.” (Genesis 1:28)
translator_notes: Augustine’s earlier text as quoted in the document Julian’s excerpts oppose. Augustine says the compiler omitted the framing about the established rule of catholic faith.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Augustine quoted in the intermediary document
english: “We say that those born from such union inherit original sin. Whatever parents they are born from, we do not deny that they are still under the devil unless they are born again in Christ.” (Genesis 2:24)
“He did not wish to be born from that same union of the two sexes.” (Genesis 1:28)
translator_notes: The first repeats 2.2.3. The second concerns Christ. Augustine says that the intervening words about rescue from darkness and transfer into Christ’s kingdom were omitted; compare Colossians 1:13. These are quotations from Augustine, not Julian’s own statements.
“Born again in Christ” echoes the teaching about new birth in John 3:3–5.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Augustine quoted in the intermediary document
english: “This shameful desire, which shameless people praise shamelessly, would not exist unless the human being had first sinned. But marriage would exist even if no one had sinned; children could have been conceived without this disease.”
translator_notes: Augustine says the document cut off his ensuing contrast between the former “body of life” and the present “body of death.” His response invokes Romans 7:23–25; those verses were not included in the excerpt itself.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: Most blessed brother, the teachers of our time, the authors of the wicked upheaval that still rages, have decided to bring insult and ruin upon the men whose holy efforts burn them, even at the cost of the ruin of the whole church. They do not understand how much honor they have given those men: they have shown that their glory could not be torn down without tearing down the catholic religion with it. For if anyone says that human beings have free will or that God creates those who are born, they are called a Caelestian and a Pelagian. So, to avoid being called heretics, people become Manichaeans. While fearing a false accusation, they fall into a real offense. They are like wild animals surrounded by feathers so that they can be driven into nets: lacking reason, empty fear pushes them into real destruction.
translator_notes: Identified by the compiler as material from the preface of the four books. The image is of hunters using feathered lines to frighten animals toward nets. Julian’s charge of Manichaeism is directed at his opponents, who deny it. Portions are repeated by Augustine at 2.3.8–9.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Intermediary compiler’s heading
english: Against those who condemn marriage and assign its fruits to the devil (Genesis 4:1).
translator_notes: Augustine expressly attributes this heading to the person who sent the excerpts, so it is preserved as the compiler’s heading, not confidently assigned to Julian.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: God, who formed Adam from mud, built Eve from a rib and said: “She will be called Life, because she is the mother of all the living” (Genesis 2:7, 22; Genesis 3:20).
From the first naming he showed the task for which she had been prepared, and said: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28).

Therefore God, the Creator of male and female, formed organs suited to procreation and arranged for bodies to be born from bodies. Yet the power of his action works in their production, governing everything that exists by the same power by which he created it.
If, then, offspring come only through sex, sex only through the body, and the body only through God, who can doubt that fruitfulness is rightly attributed to God?
translator_notes: The excerpt attributes Eve’s naming directly to God; Genesis 3:20 attributes it to Adam. Augustine notices this and allows either a lapse of memory or an interpretation that God spoke through Adam. “Life” preserves the meaning used for Eve’s name in the cited version.
Julian disputes this wording in To Florus 4.4 and supplies a longer quotation of his own text, which does not name God as the speaker.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: But you say: “Whatever parents they are born from, we do not deny that they are still under the devil unless they are born again in Christ.” (Genesis 4:25) Show, then, what the devil recognizes as his own in the sexes, through which he can rightfully possess their offspring, as you say. Is it the difference between the sexes? But that is in the bodies God made. Their union? But it is vindicated as much by the privilege of God’s blessing as by his institution. For God’s voice says: “A man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). God’s voice says: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28). Or perhaps it is fruitfulness itself? But fruitfulness is the reason marriage was instituted.
translator_notes: “Born again in Christ” echoes the teaching about new birth in John 3:3–5.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: Through what, then, are those whom God made under the devil?
“Through sin, not through nature.”
But just as there can be no offspring without the sexes, there can be no sin without the will.
For you say that they are under the devil because they are born from the union of the two sexes.
translator_notes: The second paragraph is the answer Julian supplies in his opponent’s voice. Augustine identifies it as such. The fourth is Julian’s characterization of that opponent’s position.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: Whom, then, do you confess to be the creator of infants? The true God? But he did not make evil.
[Or the devil?] But he did not create human nature.
If union is evil, the condition of bodies is shameful too; so you also assign bodies to an evil creator.
God distinguished by sex what he would unite in action. Therefore bodily union comes from the one from whom bodies originate.
So many good things—bodies, sexes, unions—cannot have evil fruits. Nor are human beings made by God so that the devil may possess them under a lawful claim, as you say (Genesis 2:24).
translator_notes: The question about the devil in brackets is reported rather than directly quoted by Augustine. The argument rejects the conclusion that bodies have an evil creator.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: After the man knew his wife through natural appetite, divine Scripture says: “Eve conceived and bore a son, and called his name Cain.” But let us hear what Adam says: “I have acquired a human being through God” (Genesis 4:1). This establishes that the person whom divine Scripture testifies was acquired through God is God’s work.
translator_notes: Genesis 4:1 assigns the statement to Eve, not Adam. The translation preserves the attribution in the surviving excerpt rather than silently correcting it.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: For Adam had fathered him through the power of his organs, not through a difference in merits.
translator_notes: Augustine explicitly says he does not understand the phrase “difference in merits.” The obscurity is present in the Latin witness and remains uncertain here.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: A little later divine Scripture says again: “Adam knew his wife Eve, and she conceived and bore a son, and called his name Seth, saying: The Lord has raised up other seed for me in place of Abel, whom Cain killed” (Genesis 4:25) (Genesis 2:7).
To demonstrate that intercourse was instituted [by God], the deity is said to have raised up the seed itself.
translator_notes: “Seed” retains the wording on which Julian’s argument depends: it can mean offspring as well as reproductive seed. Augustine objects that “raised up seed” means “gave a child,” not “aroused sexual desire.”

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: [Noah and his sons] were blessed in the same way as Adam and Eve, when God said: “Increase and multiply, fill the earth, and rule over it” (Genesis 9:1; Genesis 1:28) (1 Corinthians 15:36).

Therefore this pleasure, which you wish to make appear diabolical, was already present in the couples mentioned above. Good in its institution, it also continued under the blessing. There is no doubt that “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (1 Corinthians 15:38) was said to Noah and his sons about the union of bodies whose practice had already become established (Genesis 1:26–27) (Genesis 20:18).
translator_notes: The excerpt combines the blessing to Noah in Genesis 9:1 with language from Genesis 1:28. Both references are supplied to preserve that combination.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24) (Romans 1:27).
To state faithfully how these works take place, the prophet came close to risking modesty (Ezekiel 16:49).

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: You have certainly defined as evil by nature this desire without which there is no fruitfulness. How, then, is it aroused in old people through a heavenly gift? Now establish, if you can, that something you see God bestow as a gift belongs to the devil’s work.
translator_notes: The old couple are Abraham and Sarah receiving the promised son: Genesis 18:10–14; Romans 4:19–21. Augustine disputes Julian’s claim that the gift was desire rather than fertility.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: This union of bodies, with warmth, with pleasure, with seed, made by God, is recognized as praiseworthy within its proper measure. Sometimes it even becomes a great gift to the godly.
You must therefore confess that the original sin you invented has vanished.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: But if you say, “They still had sexual capacity, but no offspring,” (1 Corinthians 15:38) I will answer: the Creator gave the child whom the Creator promised. The child who is born is God’s work, not the work of intercourse. For he who made the first human being from dust (Genesis 2:7) forms everyone from seed. Just as the mud then taken as material was not the creator of the human being, so now that power of pleasure, producing and mixing the seed, does not itself complete the work. It offers God material from nature’s store, from which he is pleased to make a human being.
translator_notes: The passage concerns Abraham and Sarah. Its claims about the production and mixing of seed belong to ancient physiology; Augustine disputes that pleasure produces the seed.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: The apostle’s authority confirms this too. For when blessed Paul spoke of the resurrection of the dead, he said: “Fool, what you sow is not brought to life” (1 Corinthians 15:36); and below: “But God gives it a body as he wishes, and to each kind of seed its own body” (1 Corinthians 15:38). If, then, God gives human seed its own body, as he does to everything—a thing no wise or godly person denies—how will you prove that anyone is born guilty? I ask you at last to see the snares in which the claim of natural sin is strangled.

But come, I beg you, treat yourself more kindly. Believe me, God made you too; but, as must be confessed, a serious error has infected you. For what could be more irreligious than to say that God did not make the human being, or made the human being for the devil, as you say; or that the devil made God’s image, the human being (Genesis 1:26–27)? That is recognized as no less foolish than ungodly. Is God, then, so poor and so shameless that he had nothing to give holy people as a reward except what the devil poured into those he deceived as a vice?

Do you wish to know that God is shown to have given this power of procreation even to people who are not holy? When Abraham, frightened by a foreign people, called Sarah, his wife, his sister, Abimelech, the king of that region, is reported to have taken her for use at night. But God, concerned for the holy woman’s honor, came to Abimelech in a dream and restrained the king’s boldness, threatening death if he continued to violate the marriage. Then Abimelech said: “Lord, will you destroy an ignorant and righteous nation? Did they not themselves say they were brother and sister?” Abimelech rose in the morning, took a thousand silver double-drachmas, sheep, calves, male servants and female servants, and gave them to Abraham. He sent the woman away from him untouched. Abraham prayed to God for Abimelech, and God healed Abimelech, his wife, and his female servants (Genesis 20:2–7, 14–17).

At Abraham’s prayer God healed, by the power of his hidden providence, what had been removed from the sexual organs of those lowly women, because God had closed every womb in Abimelech’s household (Genesis 20:18). See, then, whether something should be called evil by nature when God sometimes removes it in anger and restores it when appeased. He makes the children of the godly and the ungodly alike. Their becoming parents belongs to nature, which rejoices in God as its Creator; their being ungodly belongs to the wickedness of their pursuits, which comes to each person from free will.
translator_notes: The intermediary excerpt omits “unless it dies” from 1 Corinthians 15:36; Augustine explicitly objects to that omission in the next section. It is preserved here as a feature of this witness, not silently repaired. The Genesis account is a free retelling and includes wording that differs from modern English versions. The awkward phrase about what was removed from the women’s organs is preserved cautiously; the argument concerns their capacity for procreation.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: Let us learn from the apostle that children born from marriage are good by nature. Speaking of the ungodly, he says: “Abandoning the natural use of the woman, they burned with desire for one another, males doing what is shameful with males” (Romans 1:27). He therefore shows that the use of the woman is natural and, within its proper bounds, praiseworthy; shameful conduct, however, is committed by a person’s own will against the modesty of the created order. So the kind of desire and its proper measure are rightly praised in those who use it well, while its excess is punished in those who act shamefully.

Indeed, at the same time that God revived Abraham’s and Sarah’s bodily organs, withered by age, he punished those same organs at Sodom with a rain of fire (Genesis 18:10–14; 19:24). If, then, you think the vigor of the organs must be condemned because through it the Sodomites became covered in shameful deeds, you will also condemn bread and wine as created things, since divine Scripture indicates that these too were means of their sin. For the Lord says through the prophet Ezekiel: “These, indeed, were the wrongs of your sister Sodom: pride; she and her children overflowed with an abundance of bread and wine, and they did not help the poor and needy” (Ezekiel 16:49). Now choose whichever you prefer: either count the bodily union as God’s work, or likewise declare bread and wine evil as created things. If you do that, you will plainly be proved a Manichaean.

Anyone who keeps natural desire within bounds uses a good thing well; anyone who fails to keep it within bounds uses a good thing badly. Why, then, do you say: “The good of marriage cannot be condemned because of the original evil derived from it, just as the evil of adultery cannot be excused by the natural good born from it”? With these words you have granted what you denied and taken away what you granted. Nothing occupies you more than making yourself hard to understand.

Show bodily marriage without sexual union, or give this activity a single name and call marriage either good or evil. You certainly promised to define marriage as good. If marriage is good, if the human being who is the fruit of marriage is good, and if this fruit, God’s work, cannot be evil when born through good from good, where, then, is the original evil that so many prior findings have ruled out?
translator_notes: The Ezekiel quotation reflects an Old Latin form that explicitly includes an abundance of wine; this differs from the wording of most modern English versions. The sentence about marriage and adultery quotes Augustine as Julian challenges him.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: By a new kind of argument, you profess to be Catholic while taking the Manichaean’s side, saying that marriage is both a great good and a great evil.
translator_notes: This is Julian’s accusation about Augustine’s position, which Augustine disputes.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: You declare a human being guiltless if born from fornication, but not innocent if born from marriage. That is where your statement leads: a natural good can arise from adultery, while original evil is derived even from marriage.
translator_notes: Julian states what he takes to be an implication of Augustine’s position. Augustine denies teaching this distinction.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: One of these statements is true; the other is false.

It is true that the person born from adultery cannot excuse the guilt of the adultery, because what the adulterers did belongs to the fault of their will; what they produced, however, deserves the praise given to fertility. If someone sows stolen wheat, the harvest that grows is not guilty. So I condemn the thief but praise the crop. I pronounce the newborn innocent on account of the good quality of the seed, as the apostle says: “God gives it a body as he wishes, and to each kind of seed its own body” (1 Corinthians 15:38). But I condemn the wrongdoer, who sinned through a perverse intention.
translator_notes: Augustine’s brief reply separates the two quoted passages; it is omitted here.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: Certainly, if evil is derived from marriage, marriages can be condemned and cannot be excused. You place their work and fruit under the devil’s authority, because every cause of evil is without good. The person born from marriage is attributed to seed, however, not to crimes. The cause of the seed lies in the constitution of bodies. Whoever misuses those bodies damages the merit of what is good, not its kind. It is therefore perfectly clear that good is not the cause of evil.

If, then, original evil is derived even from marriage, the marital union is the cause of evil, and that through which and from which an evil fruit appeared must itself be evil. As the Lord says in the Gospel: “A tree is known by its fruits” (Matthew 12:33; compare Matthew 7:16–20). Why do you think anyone should listen to you when you say that marriage is good, yet declare that nothing but evil comes from it? Marriage, then, is clearly guilty if original sin is derived from it, and it cannot be defended unless its fruit is shown to be innocent. But marriages are defended and pronounced good; their fruit is therefore shown to be innocent.
translator_notes: Julian is arguing that Augustine’s premises would condemn marriage; he himself concludes that marriage and its offspring are good.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: Through what, then, is sin found in the infant? Through the will? The infant had none. Through marriage? But marriage belongs to the parents’ activity, and you had already said that they did not sin in this act—although, from what follows, it appears you had not really granted that. Are the marriages themselves therefore to be cursed because they caused the evil? Yet they indicate only the activity of the persons involved. The parents, then, who caused sin through their union, are rightly subject to condemnation.

If we follow your view, there can now be no doubt that married people are handed over to eternal punishment, since their activity brought about the devil’s rule over human beings. And where is the statement you made a little earlier, that the human being is God’s work? For if evil enters people through their origin, and the devil gains authority over people through that evil, you are calling the devil the maker of human beings, since from him comes the origin of those being born. But if you believe that God makes the human being and that married people are innocent, see how impossible it is to maintain that original sin is derived from them (Genesis 2:24).
translator_notes: The condemnation of parents is a consequence Julian draws for argument’s sake from Augustine’s teaching, not a judgment Julian endorses.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: The one being born does not sin; the one who begot the child does not sin; the one who created the child does not sin. Through what cracks among so many defenses of innocence do you imagine that sin entered?

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: If sin comes from the will, the will that commits sin is evil. If it comes from nature, nature is evil.
If nature is God’s work, the devil’s work is not allowed to pass through God’s work (John 1:3).
translator_notes: Two separate quoted statements occur in Augustine’s discussion; his intervening reply is omitted.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: In one person, the intention is rightly condemned and the origin praised, because there are two things to which opposite judgments can be applied. In an infant, however, there is only one thing: nature alone, because there is no will. That one thing, then, must be assigned either to God or to a demon. If nature comes through God, there can be no original evil in it. If it comes from the devil, there will be no basis for claiming the human being as God’s work. Thus anyone who defends original evil is thoroughly Manichaean.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: Again you say: “There would be no desire if the human being had not first sinned, but marriage would exist even if no one had sinned.”
translator_notes: Julian quotes Augustine here. Augustine objects that his actual wording was “no shameful desire,” not “no desire.” This witness preserves Julian’s shortened form.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: Those marriages, then, which you say could have existed without desire, without bodily movement, and without the need for the sexes, are pronounced praiseworthy by you. But the marriages now taking place you declare to have been invented by the devil. Those which you dream could have been instituted you judge good. But the marriages of which divine Scripture says, “A man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24), you profess to be evils of the devil. In the end, you say they ought to be called a disease rather than marriage.
translator_notes: This is Julian’s portrayal of Augustine’s position. Augustine denies saying that marriage could exist without bodily movement or the two sexes, and denies that present marriages were invented by the devil.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: You say, then, that those who were never born could have been good. But those who have filled the world, for whom Christ died, you declare to be the devil’s work, born from a disease, and guilty from the beginning. I have therefore proved that all you are doing is denying that God created the human beings who actually exist.
translator_notes: Julian is accusing Augustine, not denying creation himself. “For whom Christ died” is a clear Pauline echo; compare Romans 14:15 and 1 Corinthians 8:11. Augustine repeats this quotation in 2.33.56 and bases his reply on it.

work: To Turbantius: extracts in On Marriage and Concupiscence
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
english: If, before sin, God created what human beings would be born from, but the devil supplied what would arouse their parents, holiness will undoubtedly be assigned to the newborn and guilt to those who beget them. Since this most clearly condemns marriage, please remove this view from the churches’ midst. Truly believe that through Jesus Christ all things were made, and without him nothing was made (John 1:3).
translator_notes: This is the final excerpt in the intermediary document, according to Augustine at 2.35.60, where its closing sentence is repeated.
